blocks.text: Third John is a brief personal letter that reflects internal conflict within a Christian community. Unlike longer epistles, this letter does not identify its writer by personal name, location, or destination. The sender identifies himself only as 'the elder' and addresses an individual named Gaius. The letter commends Gaius for his hospitality toward traveling missionaries while sharply criticizing Diotrephes, who refuses to receive them.

The letter opens with 'the elder' addressing Gaius as 'beloved' and declaring his love for him 'in truth.' Following this personal greeting, the elder expresses a comprehensive wish for Gaius's welfare: that he prosper in all things and enjoy good health, even as his soul flourishes. This parallel between physical health and spiritual condition suggests the elder views Gaius as a person of spiritual maturity whose outward circumstances should match his inner well-being.

The elder reports great joy upon hearing from traveling believers who testified to Gaius's faithfulness. They witnessed that Gaius 'walks in truth'—language denoting not merely intellectual assent but lived conduct aligned with truth. This delight culminates in the elder's declaration that his greatest happiness is hearing of his spiritual 'children' walking in truth. The metaphor of 'children' reflects early Christian convention whereby spiritual leaders spoke of their converts or those they nurtured as their spiritual offspring.

The elder commends Gaius for his faithful work extending hospitality to both 'brethren and strangers'—distinguishing between known believers and traveling visitors previously unknown to him. This generosity came to public attention when the travelers testified before the church about Gaius's love. The elder then encourages Gaius to send these missionaries onward on their journey in a manner 'worthy of God,' implying that the treatment of such itinerants reflects one's alignment with divine values.

These travelers had gone out 'for the Name,' an expression the letter leaves unexplained. Notably, they refused to accept support from non-believers, demonstrating both their commitment and independence from outside patronage. The elder frames the support of such travelers as a shared responsibility: 'We therefore ought to welcome such, that we may be fellow-workers for the truth.' By providing hospitality, Gaius becomes a participant in their mission.

The letter's tone shifts sharply when introducing a serious problem within the community. The elder had written previously to the church, but now addresses a figure named Diotrephes who 'loves to have the preeminence among them.' This desire for first place has apparently led to open conflict: Diotrephes refuses to receive the elder and his associates. The elder accuses Diotrephes of making malicious accusations against them and, more gravely, of refusing to welcome the traveling believers and actively hindering others in the church who wish to receive them. The elder warns that he anticipates a visit during which he will confront these actions.

The elder returns to direct moral instruction, telling Gaius: 'Imitate not that which is evil, but that which is good.' He grounds this in a theological principle: 'He that doeth good is of God; he that doeth evil hath not seen God.' This claim suggests that actions reveal one's spiritual standing and relationship with the divine. By contrast to Diotrephes, the elder then commends Demetrius, who receives testimony from 'all men, and of the truth itself,' with the elder and associates adding their own witness. This layered testimony—from all, from truth itself, and from the elder's circle—establishes Demetrius as trustworthy and worthy of reception.

The elder explains his brevity: he has much to write but prefers not to commit these matters to ink and pen. Instead, he expresses hope for a soon visit to Gaius, where they can speak 'face to face'—an intimate mode of communication far preferable to written correspondence. The letter concludes with a wish of peace and greetings from 'the friends,' with a request to greet them by name in return. This personal, relational closing underscores the letter's emphasis on community bonds and direct encounter as superior to written mediation.
